result.markdown: --- title: "Take-home Exercise 2 - Technical Report" author: "Jin Jiaying" date: "03 Oct 2026" date-modified: last-modified --- # 1 Overview This technical report examines the spatial and spatio-temporal patterns of political violence in Myanmar from January 2021 to September 2025. Using event-level data from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project [**(ACLED)**](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/download-data) and township administrative boundaries from the Myanmar Information Management Unit [**(MIMU)**](https://data.themimu.info/en/dataset/myanmar-administrative-boundary), the analysis is conducted at the township level to investigate how conflict events are distributed, clustered, and evolving across space and time. The analytical framework consists of three complementary components. First, Local Measures of Spatial Association (LISA), including Local Moran's I and Getis-Ord Gi*, are applied to identify statistically significant spatial clusters, hot spots, cold spots, and spatial outliers. Second, Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) examines the evolution of spatial concentrations across monthly observations. Third, spatially constrained clustering is employed to identify geographically connected townships with similar historical patterns of recorded political violence. Together, these approaches provide a more comprehensive understanding of where violence is concentrated, how these concentrations evolve over time, and how neighbouring townships can be grouped into meaningful geographical regions. # 2 Introduction and Study Context Myanmar has experienced decades of political instability and ethnic conflict, with longstanding tensions over political authority, ethnic autonomy, and territorial control. As documented by the [Council on Foreign Relations (CFR)](https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/rohingya-crisis-myanmar), these conflicts have deep historical roots extending well before the military takeover in February 2021. Following the coup, armed resistance expanded across multiple states and regions, intensifying the country's humanitarian and security challenges. By February 2025, more than 3.5 million people were estimated to be internally displaced, highlighting the scale of the ongoing humanitarian crisis ([OCHA, 2025](https://myanmar.un.org/en/289497-myanmar-humanitarian-update-no-44)). The conflict landscape has also become increasingly fragmented. An [ACLED report on resistance groups in Myanmar](https://acleddata.com/report/between-cooperation-and-competition-struggle-resistance-groups-myanmar) highlights the complex relationships between established Ethnic Armed Organisations (EAOs) and newer resistance groups, including patterns of cooperation, competition, and territorial disputes. These dynamics differ across geographical areas, suggesting that political violence may exhibit distinct spatial concentrations and changing patterns over time. However, political violence is not evenly distributed across Myanmar. The frequency and geographical concentration of recorded conflict events may vary substantially between townships and across different periods. National-level summaries may therefore conceal important localised patterns, while cumulative event counts alone may overlook emerging or changing concentrations of violence. Examining neighbouring townships and temporal variations can provide a more comprehensive understanding of these geographical differences. Against this background, this study examines recorded political violence across Myanmar's townships from January 2021 to September 2025. It applies Local Measures of Spatial Association (LISA and Getis-Ord Gi*) to identify significant spatial concentrations and outliers, Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) to investigate their temporal evolution, and Spatially Constrained Clustering to identify geographically connected areas with similar historical violence patterns. By integrating these approaches, the study aims to provide a geographically informed perspective that can support conflict monitoring and humanitarian planning. # 3 Research Questions and Objectives ## 3.1 Research Questions This study aims to understand both the spatial concentration and temporal evolution of political violence across Myanmar at the township level. It addresses the following research questions: **Q1 — Concentration:** Where are significant spatial clusters, hot spots, cold spots, and spatial outliers of recorded political violence located across Myanmar townships? **Q2 — Spatio-temporal Evolution:** How have spatial concentrations of recorded political violence evolved between January 2021 and September 2025? **Q3 — Spatially Constrained Regional Patterns:** Can geographically contiguous townships be grouped into meaningful regions based on similarities in their historical violence patterns? **Q4 — Practical Implications:** How can the combined spatial, temporal, and regional findings support geographically informed conflict monitoring and humanitarian planning? ## 3.2 Research Objectives To address these questions, the study aims to: 1. **Identify spatial concentrations and anomalies** of political violence using township-level spatial association and hot spot analysis. 2. **Examine the evolution of conflict hot spots over time** to distinguish temporary concentrations from persistent or changing patterns. 3. **Integrate spatial and temporal findings** to develop a clearer understanding of where political violence is concentrated and how these areas are changing. 4. **Support geographic prioritisation and decision-making** by identifying townships that may warrant closer monitoring or attention, providing spatial evidence that can inform conflict monitoring, humanitarian planning, resource prioritisation, and peace-building initiatives. ## 3.3 Practical Relevance The practical value of this analysis lies not only in identifying where conflict events are concentrated, but also in distinguishing areas with different spatial and temporal trajectories. For example, a persistent hot spot may indicate a location requiring sustained monitoring, while an emerging or intensifying hot spot may signal an area where attention is becoming increasingly important. Conversely, diminishing hot spots may indicate changing conflict dynamics that warrant further investigation. These insights can provide an evidence-based geographical perspective for organisations involved in conflict monitoring, humanitarian response, public safety, and peace-building. The analysis is intended to support prioritisation rather than predict individual conflict events or establish the causes of violence. # 4 Data and Study Design ## 4.1 Data Sources This study integrates two geospatial datasets. Political violence events are obtained from the **ACLED** (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project), which provides event-level information including event date, event type, geographic coordinates, administrative location, and reported fatalities. Township administrative boundaries are obtained from the **MIMU** (Myanmar Information Management Unit) administrative boundary dataset. The ACLED dataset covers events recorded between **1 January 2021 and 30 September 2025**, while the MIMU dataset provides the spatial boundaries of **330 townships** across Myanmar. ## 4.2 Spatial and Temporal Units of Analysis The **township (ADM3)** is selected as the primary spatial unit of analysis. Township-level analysis provides sufficient geographical detail to identify localised patterns while maintaining a consistent administrative unit that can support comparison across Myanmar. The study covers 57 monthly periods between January 2021 and September 2025. Monthly aggregation is adopted to capture short-term fluctuations and longer-term changes in recorded political violence. Since 2025 includes only nine months of observations, comparisons of annual event totals may be misleading. Therefore, average monthly event frequency is used for comparisons across years, while equivalent January–September observation windows are examined as an additional consistency check. For the spatial clustering analysis, year-specific average monthly event frequencies are used to represent each township's historical violence profile. For EHSA, the complete monthly panel is retained to investigate the evolution of local hot and cold spots. ## 4.3 Definition of Political Violence This study operationalises political violence using the frequency of recorded conflict events rather than their severity or reported fatalities. The primary measure includes three ACLED event types: Battles, Explosions/Remote violence, and Violence against civilians. Each recorded event contributes equally to the event count. The event_type classification is selected as the primary analytical level, focusing on Battles, Explosions/Remote violence, and Violence against civilians. The broader disorder_type classification is reviewed descriptively to assess differences in event coverage. However, the spatial analyses are conducted using the selected event_type definition only. Accordingly, the term "violence level" in this report refers to recorded political violence event frequency, rather than a direct measure of casualties, severity, or population-level risk. ## 4.4 Study Design The study adopts an **observational geospatial and spatio-temporal analytical design**. It examines recorded patterns of political violence rather than attempting to establish causal relationships between conflict and external socioeconomic or political factors. The analytical design combines three perspectives. First, LISA and Getis-Ord Gi* identify spatial concentrations and outliers across the study period. Second, EHSA examines changes in local hot and cold spot patterns using monthly observations. Third, SKATER groups geographically connected townships with similar historical violence profiles. Together, these approaches provide complementary insights into spatial concentration, temporal behaviour, and regional similarity. # 5 Loading Necessary R Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(sf, sfdep, spdep, tidyverse, tmap, plotly, Kendall, knitr) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: R packages used in this analysis |Package |Purpose | |:---------|:------------------------------------------------------| |sf |Spatial data handling | |sfdep |Spatial dependence and hot spot analysis | |spdep |Spatial neighbours, weights and constrained clustering | |tidyverse |Data wrangling and visualisation | |tmap |Thematic mapping | |plotly |Interactive visualisation | |Kendall |Mann-Kendall trend analysis | |knitr |Table formatting | ::: ::: # 6 Data preparation and quality assessment ## Importantly, coldspot classifications indicate relatively low spatial concentrations of recorded events during particular periods, rather than an absence of conflict or evidence of safety. # 12 Spatially Constrained Clustering ## 12.1 Methodology and Feature Selection Spatially Constrained Clustering is performed using the SKATER algorithm to identify geographically contiguous townships with similar historical patterns of recorded political violence. Unlike LISA and Gi*, SKATER is an unsupervised clustering method rather than a statistical significance test. It incorporates both spatial adjacency and attribute similarity to form geographically connected groups. Six temporal features are selected: the average monthly event frequency for each year from 2021 to 2025, and the proportion of months with at least one recorded event. Three isolated townships were excluded from neighbour-based analyses. SKATER clustering also depends on the selected temporal features and number of clusters. **Interpretation Limitations:** Spatial associations and temporal patterns do not establish causal relationships.
